sections.lever checks:
- Family and target: a per-firm limit from one response turned into audits that must change hands, timed at the yearly rate another response's estimate implies; medium. Measured so far: rev 0 failed the closed-book gate (see Repair in rev 1); no solver tier has been measured on any revision.
- Repair in rev 1 (2026-10-12): rev 0 asked only for the years and its gold, "7 years", was reached by the platform's no-document attempt as a guess from the rounding instruction (Feedback log). One change: the question now also asks for the number of audits the cap allows the Big Four between them (260), a figure that exists only through Doc 6's 65. The years ask, its rate, its rounding and both ticked documents are unchanged. The added part does not point at the silent offset (the 11 audits already held), so the route that forgets it is still open (aq-02360 q01's lesson: a non-guessable addition must not tie the trap).
- Dependency plan: D06 L282 (65 per Big Four firm) -> 4 × 65 = 260 (c1). D02 L616 (11 audits held by other firms, about 60 wins in five years) -> 350 − 11 = 339 held by the Big Four -> 339 − 260 = 79 to give up; 60 / 5 = 12 a year; 79 / 12 = 6.58 -> 7 years (c2). Minimal inputs: 65, 11, 60 wins, five years; 350 from the index's name.
- Universe: not applicable (two derived numbers).
- Necessity: D06 supplies the individual cap of 65, needed for both parts; the only other per-firm limits in the bundle are BDO's own 60 and "say 50" (D01 L145, L221), a different respondent's proposal, and ICAEW's collective "around 60%" (D06 L408), which the question excludes by "individual". D02 supplies the rate (about 60 tender wins in five years) and the 11 audits held, needed for the years; a search of all ten documents for tender counts finds only D04 note 4 (8 of 29 tendering companies changed auditor), which gives no forward rate. Without D06 neither part can be formed; without D02 there is no rate. No removal probes run (optional diagnostics, none requested).
- Bundle independence (closed-book): the question prints 350, "five-year" and "Big Four". Numbers a guesser could form from them: 350 / 5 = 70, 350 / 4 = 87.5, 350 − 70 = 280, 350 × 4 / 5 = 280, 350 − 87.5 = 262.5; none is 260 (262.5 is the nearest and is not a whole number of audits). The years part alone remains guessable, as rev 0 showed; the answer is right only with both parts.
- Selected-lever checks: not a which-items question, no decoy required. State the rounding: 6.58 rounds to 7; one decimal place would split the stated bases (6.6 and 6.7), so whole years is the supported precision.
- Targeted failure modes: (1) Part vs total: the Big Four taken to hold the whole index, 350 − 260 = 90 audits, 90 / 12 = 7.5, given as 8 years (answer "260 and 8"), when other firms already hold 11 (D02 L616, the paragraph that gives the rate). (2) Look-alike measure: ICAEW's collective cap "of around 60%" (D06 L408, Appendix A): 60% of 350 = 210 audits, 339 − 210 = 129, 129 / 12 = 10.75, 11 years (answer "210 and 11"). Considered and not declared: scaling the five years by 90 / 70 = 6.43, 6 years (no trap definition names a proportional short cut); reading 65 companies as 65% (227.5 audits; the paragraph says "65 of the FTSE 350 companies"); adding D02 L91's "one to two years before these audits go live" (the question asks for years of wins). No solver attempt with documents has been measured: align the modes with the next run's observed wrong answers before Submit.
- Calculation verification: script, 2026-10-12: 4 × 65 = 260; 350 − 11 = 339; 339 − 260 = 79; 60 / 5 = 12; 79 / 12 = 6.583; 12 × 6 = 72; 79 − 72 = 7 > 6. Units: audits (companies), tender wins, years. Rounding to the nearest whole year, half-up or half-even alike.
- Semantic/ID/overview probes: bundle overview lists "65 clients market cap", "60% collective Big Four market share cap", "20% target for FTSE350 audits by outside firms" and "60% of all tenders required to reach target"; none gives 260, 11, 60 tenders, 79 or 7. Searches: "65" (D06 L53, L282 only), "260" (no hit in any document), "tender" with figures (D02, D04 note 4), "audits of the FTSE 350" (D02 L616). Shortest complete route found is the eight steps above.
- Precision/readings: c1 has one reading (4 × 65; D06 L53 "around 65 clients for any single firm" and L282 "65 of the FTSE 350 companies" agree). For c2 the present audits outside the Big Four are stated as 11 (D02 L616), 3% (D02 L254, 10.5), 98% inside (D02 L67, 7) and by "sevenfold" (D02 L89, 10); with each base's own five-year wins (59 to 63) the result is 6.58, 6.68, 6.59, 6.67 years, and 6.69 with exactly 59 wins: 7 on every one. Mixed inputs (83 audits at 12 a year) give 6.92: still 7. "would bring them within it" is the least time, every Big Four firm at its cap; the bundle gives no per-firm holdings.
- Completeness: no known source gaps (10 of 10 documents read in full; hashes match the capture).
- Style/set review: plain wording, respondents named as organisations, no file or page references; 40 words, two parallel asks. Only question on this bundle; i02 uses the same Deloitte paragraph and is an alternate, not a second question.
- Warnings answered: origin claude (the form's authorship tick is the user's). form-numbers: Step 3's 11 is printed at D02 character 83,552, beyond the range the form reads: expected false alarm, quoted in Evidence.

sections.question: How many FTSE 350 audits would ICAEW's individual cap allow the Big Four between them, and how many years of tender wins, at the yearly rate Deloitte's five-year target assumes, would bring them within it, to the nearest whole year?
sections.reasoning:
Step 1. Source input (Doc 6, reply on how a cap should be measured): besides a collective cap, ICAEW describes an individual one, under which each Big Four firm could be restricted to auditing 65 of the FTSE 350 companies.
Step 2. Calculation (Doc 6): with every Big Four firm at that cap, the four together could audit 4 × 65 = 260 companies, which is the first answer.
Step 3. Source input (Doc 2, appendix reply on whether a cap's benefits could be realised): firms outside the four largest currently perform 11 audits of the FTSE 350. To hold a 20% share in the next five years they would need to win about 60 tenders.
Step 4. Calculation (Doc 2 and Doc 6): the Big Four audit the rest of the index today: 350 − 11 = 339 companies.
Step 5. Calculation (Doc 2 and Doc 6): to come within the cap they would have to give up 339 − 260 = 79 audits, each one a tender won by another firm.
Step 6. Calculation (Doc 2): the target's wins spread over its five years give a yearly rate of 60 / 5 = 12 wins.
Step 7. Calculation (Doc 2 and Doc 6): six years at that rate bring 12 × 6 = 72 wins.
Step 8. Final answer (Doc 2 and Doc 6): 79 − 72 = 7 wins are still missing after six years, more than half of one year's 12, so the time needed is closer to seven years than to six: 7 years to the nearest whole year. With the cap total from Step 2, the answer is 260 audits and 7 years.

### Failure mode 1
Trap: Part vs total
How a careless solver fails: Takes the wrong line item

### Failure mode 2
Trap: Look-alike measure
How a careless solver fails: Takes the wrong line item

Why these are traps: Part vs total: Doc 2 says other firms already perform 11 FTSE 350 audits; treating the whole index as the Big Four's gives 90 audits to shed and 8 years. Look-alike measure: Doc 6's summary gives a collective cap of around 60%: 210 audits, 11 years. The gold sheds 79.
